# Weekly Market Briefing: Software Unwinds, Semis Surge, and Factor Crowding Gets Tested

The past week on the watchlist was defined by a sharp factor reversal: high-duration, richly valued software and marketing technology sold off aggressively, while semiconductors, select industrials, data-center infrastructure, and energy outperformed. Across our 184-name universe, downside volatility was concentrated in application software, digital marketing, and fintech, with double-digit weekly drawdowns in flagship names like Atlassian, HubSpot, Intuit, Wix, and the marketing automation cohort (Braze, Klaviyo, Zeta). In contrast, semiconductors and adjacent infrastructure—anchored by Advanced Micro Devices, Taiwan Semiconductor, Micron, Vertiv, Onto Innovation, and several smaller enablers—extended their leadership, suggesting that the market is rotating within the “AI trade” rather than abandoning it. Against a backdrop of no imminent earnings catalysts over the next two weeks, price action was driven less by idiosyncratic news and more by valuation, factor exposure, and positioning normalization after a long stretch of outperformance for software and growth.

## Market Overview

This week’s tape across the watchlist was bifurcated, with software and marketing technology bearing the brunt of de-risking while semiconductors, selective industrials, and hard-asset cyclicals moved higher. At the index level we do not have authoritative data within the last week, but the internal breadth of our universe signals a rotation away from crowded growth factors and toward cyclicals and AI hardware. The most notable theme was the magnitude and breadth of the drawdown across higher-multiple software and application platforms, many of which saw weekly declines in the mid-teens without a corresponding deterioration in near-term fundamentals. Instead, the moves are best interpreted as a valuation and positioning reset, especially given the absence of upcoming earnings catalysts over the next 14 days for any watchlist names. The result is a market profile that still favors AI and data-center infrastructure exposure but is increasingly discriminating against long-duration, premium multiple software where growth differentials may not justify the spread.

Within this context, the dispersion in weekly performance is striking. On the downside, Braze declined by approximately 23.4 percent over the week and 33.7 percent over the month, placing it among the most severe drawdowns across the watchlist and signaling a decisive de-risking in marketing technology exposure. Atlassian fell about 19.0 percent on the week and 26.8 percent on the month, DocuSign declined roughly 17.6 percent over the week, and Wix lost 16.4 percent, with similar mid-teens drops in HubSpot, Intuit, Asana, monday.com, and a wide swath of enterprise software names. On the upside, Sable Offshore gained approximately 18.3 percent this week and 120.1 percent over the past month, illustrating the ongoing appetite for select energy and offshore exposure. Semiconductors were another bright spot, with Onto Innovation up 16.1 percent this week and 49.3 percent over a month, Advanced Micro Devices higher by 14.1 percent over the week and 17.0 percent over the month, and Micron up 5.1 percent weekly and 60.9 percent over the month. These moves underscore a regime where cyclicality and AI hardware remain key leadership pockets while growth software undergoes multiple compression.

From a factor lens, this pattern is consistent with a shift away from high-duration, interest-rate-sensitive growth stocks toward more tangible cash-flow generators and cyclical beneficiaries tied to capex and AI infrastructure. The sell-off in the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF proxy, which declined about 6.4 percent this week and 6.1 percent over the month, mirrors the drawdown across our software subset. Meanwhile, the strength in data storage names like Western Digital, up 10.5 percent on the week and 33.2 percent over the month, and Seagate, up 7.3 percent weekly and 17.5 percent monthly, further illustrates the market’s preference for direct beneficiaries of data growth and AI workloads. The absence of watchlist earnings in the coming two weeks reinforces the interpretation that investors are repositioning largely on valuation and macro narratives, rather than reacting to incremental company-specific information.

For portfolio construction, this market backdrop suggests that risk is shifting from idiosyncratic earnings misses toward systemic factor exposures. Portfolios that are overweight application software, digital marketing, and high-multiple fintech are likely experiencing outsized drawdowns with limited company-specific news to point to, which can challenge client narratives but simultaneously create opportunities to upgrade quality within those cohorts. Meanwhile, investors with structural exposure to semiconductors, data-center infrastructure, and select industrials tied to capex and electrification are seeing their thesis reinforced. The key challenge now is to discern whether the software de-rating is a transient positioning event or the start of a longer regime where investors demand a higher margin of safety on growth multiples. In the absence of new macro data in this report, we frame the moves as a necessary rebalancing of crowded trades at a time when AI hardware and hard-asset cyclicals continue to capture incremental capital.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

### Software Infrastructure vs. Application Software

The most pronounced rotation this week occurred within the broader software complex, where both infrastructure and application software underperformed but with differing degrees and narratives. Application software experienced acute pressure: Atlassian declined approximately 19.0 percent over the week and 26.8 percent over the month, DocuSign fell 17.6 percent weekly, ServiceTitan dropped 16.9 percent, HubSpot was down 16.1 percent, Intuit and Asana both fell 15.7 percent, Constellation Software declined 14.4 percent, and monday.com also lost 14.4 percent. These are material drawdowns within a single week and follow a month in which most of these names have already corrected by mid-teens percentages, suggesting that a multi-week re-rating of application software valuations is underway.

Software infrastructure, while also under pressure, exhibited a somewhat more nuanced picture. Nutanix declined about 14.5 percent on the week and 8.9 percent on the month, signaling renewed skepticism around the durability of its growth narrative and the sustainability of its valuation. UiPath fell 12.1 percent weekly and 10.2 percent monthly, indicating investor concerns around automation software’s competitive intensity and monetization timeline. Elastic dropped 9.2 percent over the week, while Amplitude declined 8.7 percent, and Trimble fell 8.3 percent in the same period. Yet within this cohort, Everpure (PSTG) gained 8.8 percent on the week and 9.9 percent over the month, and Vertiv rose 8.2 percent weekly and 18.1 percent monthly, demonstrating that investors are differentiating between pure-play software and firms that sit closer to infrastructure hardware, data-center spending, or mission-critical workflows.

In the aggregate, the decline of roughly 6.4 percent this week in the broad software proxy, paired with the mid-teens drawdowns in flagship application platforms, shows the market’s willingness to compress multiples where growth visibility is strong but valuations have outrun fundamentals. The variability within infrastructure software—where certain names like Vertiv and Everpure are rewarded while others like Nutanix and UiPath are punished—reflects a more discerning framework that favors companies with direct exposure to AI infrastructure, power management, and storage rather than pure software abstractions. For investors, this argues for leaning into infrastructure and hardware-adjacent names within the software stack while being more selective and valuation-sensitive in application software.

### Cybersecurity and Data & Analytics

Cybersecurity, which had been a relative safe harbor during prior growth rotations, was not immune to this week’s de-risking, though the drawdowns were generally less severe than in application software. Rapid7 declined approximately 10.3 percent on the week and 19.2 percent over the month, a notable underperformance that suggests investors remain concerned about its path to scale and margin expansion. SentinelOne fell 8.1 percent weekly and 4.0 percent monthly, while Tenable, Varonis, and Rubrik each saw weekly declines of around 4.9 percent. Fortinet lost 4.8 percent on the week, Check Point fell 3.7 percent, and CrowdStrike declined 3.5 percent in the same period. These moves, while painful, are more contained relative to the mid-teens declines elsewhere in software, underscoring that security remains a favored subtheme even amid broader risk-off sentiment toward growth.

Data and analytics names also came under pressure, reflecting their status as high-multiple beneficiaries of the AI narrative. Elastic, as noted, fell 9.2 percent over the week and 4.2 percent over the month, while Amplitude dropped 8.7 percent weekly and 13.4 percent monthly. Dynatrace declined 5.7 percent this week and 9.2 percent over the month, and Fair Isaac fell 5.9 percent weekly and 10.7 percent monthly. These names are often priced for durable double-digit growth, and the recent drawdowns indicate that investors are increasingly unwilling to pay peak multiples for growth that, while strong, may no longer be accelerating. At the same time, the performance gap between security and broader analytics suggests that investors still prioritize mission-critical security spend over discretionary analytics or experimentation tooling.

For portfolio positioning, this dynamic implies that cybersecurity can remain a core overweight within software, but selectivity is key. Higher-beta names like Rapid7 may remain vulnerable until there is clearer evidence of a re-acceleration in growth or a credible path to margin expansion. In data and analytics, the correction in Elastic, Dynatrace, and Amplitude creates a more attractive entry point for long-term investors, but near-term performance is likely to remain tied to the broader risk appetite for high-multiple growth. The key will be to differentiate between businesses that are structurally embedded in customer workflows and those whose tools remain more discretionary.

### Semiconductors, Storage, and AI Infrastructure

In stark contrast to software, semiconductors and related hardware continued to lead this week, reinforcing the market’s conviction in the AI infrastructure build-out. Onto Innovation rose approximately 16.1 percent this week and 49.3 percent over the month, making it one of the strongest performers on the watchlist and highlighting investor enthusiasm for front-end and process control equipment tied to advanced node production. Advanced Micro Devices gained 14.1 percent on the week and 17.0 percent over the month, benefiting from ongoing optimism around its GPU and accelerator roadmap. POET Technologies advanced 12.3 percent this week and 39.0 percent over the month, while Astera Labs (ALAB) climbed 11.9 percent weekly and 29.8 percent monthly, each reflecting bullish positioning around connectivity and interconnect solutions critical to AI data centers.

The strength extended into storage and memory, where Western Digital rose 10.5 percent on the week and 33.2 percent over the month, and Seagate gained 7.3 percent weekly and 17.5 percent monthly. Micron, a key beneficiary of high-bandwidth memory demand, was up 5.1 percent this week and an impressive 60.9 percent over the month. SNDK, within the data storage cohort, gained 9.6 percent weekly and 100.0 percent over the month, albeit off a smaller base, underscoring the intensity of investor interest in storage-related plays. Taiwan Semiconductor added 5.8 percent this week and 23.6 percent over the month, while Teradyne gained 5.0 percent weekly and 23.2 percent monthly, rounding out a strong month for semis across the value chain.

Data-center infrastructure and power also participated in the upside. Vertiv, which sits at the nexus of power, cooling, and data-center infrastructure, rose approximately 8.2 percent this week and 18.1 percent over the month, continuing its steady climb as investors increasingly focus on the physical constraints of AI capacity expansion. Corning, with exposure to optical connectivity and specialty glass, gained 10.5 percent weekly and 10.3 percent monthly, while GE Vernova advanced 9.5 percent over the week and 11.0 percent over the month, and Generac rose 5.3 percent weekly and 11.1 percent monthly. Together, these moves suggest that the market is expanding its AI-related opportunity set beyond chips into the enabling infrastructure—power, cooling, optics, and materials—required to support the next wave of compute growth.

For investors, the message is clear: the AI trade has rotated decisively toward hardware, memory, and infrastructure, and that rotation remained intact this week despite volatility in software. The challenge is valuation, especially after monthly moves as strong as 60.9 percent for Micron and 49.3 percent for Onto Innovation. Near term, we would expect bouts of profit-taking, but structurally the demand backdrop for AI compute, memory, and data-center infrastructure remains supportive. Portfolio strategy should emphasize a barbell between core, high-liquidity leaders like Taiwan Semiconductor and Advanced Micro Devices, and more idiosyncratic enablers such as Astera Labs, Onto Innovation, and leading storage names, while remaining disciplined on position sizing given elevated volatility.

### Energy, Industrials, and Cyclicals

Energy and industrials continued to show resilience, offering diversification benefits against the drawdown in growth software. Sable Offshore advanced approximately 18.3 percent this week and 120.1 percent over the month, making it one of the most explosive performers on the watchlist. This reflects not only company-specific momentum but also the market’s broader interest in offshore and energy infrastructure in a world where energy security and longer-cycle projects retain strategic importance. Comfort Systems USA gained 10.8 percent weekly and 26.7 percent monthly, a notable performance for an industrial tied to mechanical and HVAC systems, and likely a derivative play on construction, data-center build-outs, and infrastructure upgrades.

Within industrials and materials, Corning’s 10.5 percent weekly and 10.3 percent monthly gains, GE Vernova’s 9.5 percent and 11.0 percent respective moves, CNH Industrial’s 7.2 percent weekly and 14.0 percent monthly increase, and Nucor’s 6.5 percent weekly and 8.5 percent monthly rise all suggest that investors are incrementally rewarding companies with exposure to capex, infrastructure, electrification, and industrial activity. California Resources gained 5.3 percent this week and 5.4 percent over the month, rounding out a constructive backdrop for select energy and resource names. The outperformance of these cyclical and hard-asset exposures provides a partial hedge against multiple compression in long-duration growth and indicates that the market is willing to fund real-asset plays alongside AI infrastructure.

For portfolio construction, this sector leadership supports a tilt toward quality cyclicals as a complement to AI hardware. Names like Nucor, GE Vernova, Comfort Systems, and CNH offer exposure to industrial and infrastructure end markets that can benefit from both private and public capex. Energy exposures through Sable Offshore and California Resources add torque to rising demand and constrained capacity environments. The risk, as always, lies in the sensitivity of these names to macro growth and commodity cycles, but the recent performance dynamics suggest that investors are using them as a relative safe harbor amid volatility in higher-multiple growth.

### Financials, Fintech, and Consumer

Financials and fintech were relative laggards this week, reflecting cyclical concerns and risk-off sentiment toward consumer-exposed credit and payments. Among the large diversified banks on the watchlist, Wells Fargo declined approximately 7.9 percent this week and 4.5 percent over the month, Bank of America fell 5.2 percent weekly and 2.9 percent monthly, and JPMorgan declined 5.1 percent on the week and 0.8 percent over the month. Within consumer finance, Synchrony Financial dropped 7.7 percent weekly and 3.6 percent monthly, while Global Payments fell 7.2 percent on the week and 10.2 percent over the month. These moves suggest that investors remain cautious on credit quality, loan growth, and the overall macro trajectory, even though we do not have specific macro data within this report.

Fintech-specific names also came under pressure. BILL Holdings declined approximately 14.5 percent this week and 12.5 percent over the month, a meaningful drawdown that raises questions about investor confidence in its profitability trajectory and competitive positioning. Affirm fell 8.6 percent weekly but is still up 3.8 percent over the month, indicating that buy-now-pay-later sentiment remains volatile but not uniformly bearish. Block, referenced here as XYZ, declined 5.2 percent over the week but remains up 3.4 percent over the month, while LPL Financial gained 5.2 percent weekly and 6.4 percent monthly, illustrating that fee-based advisory and wealth platforms can still attract capital even as credit and payments face headwinds.

Consumer and e-commerce names delivered a mixed picture. Wix declined approximately 16.4 percent this week and 22.9 percent over the month, Global-E fell 9.8 percent weekly and 5.5 percent monthly, Sea Limited dropped 9.1 percent in the week but remains up 2.1 percent over the month, and GoDaddy was down 8.0 percent weekly and 16.8 percent monthly. Shopify fell 5.3 percent and is down 3.7 percent over the month. In contrast, Constellation Brands rose 6.6 percent weekly and 12.1 percent monthly, Mondelez gained 3.9 percent, and Clorox advanced 3.6 percent over the month, pointing to a relative bid for defensive consumer staples. The dispersion within consumer-related names reinforces the need to differentiate between discretionary, rate-sensitive business models and defensive, staple-like cash flow streams.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

### Biggest Decliners: Software and Marketing Tech Under Pressure

The largest negative outliers this week were concentrated in application software and marketing technology, underscoring a pronounced de-risking within those segments. Braze declined about 23.4 percent over the week and 33.7 percent over the month, making it the single worst performer on the watchlist in that period. This magnitude of drawdown, in the absence of fresh earnings, suggests a combination of multiple compression and investor concern about competitive intensity in customer engagement platforms. Given Braze’s profile as a high-growth, high-multiple name, the market appears to be recalibrating the acceptable premium for such growth, especially as adjacent marketing technology names also sold off.

Atlassian’s 19.0 percent weekly decline and 26.8 percent monthly drawdown place it among the most impacted enterprise software names. The move likely reflects concerns about the sustainability of its growth rates, the pace of cloud migrations, and the degree to which its valuation had already priced in long-term free cash flow expansion. DocuSign, down 17.6 percent this week and 16.3 percent over the month, similarly illustrates investor skepticism about post-pandemic growth and margin profiles. ServiceTitan’s 16.9 percent weekly drop, HubSpot’s 16.1 percent decline, and Intuit’s 15.7 percent fall, along with Asana and monday.com each losing 15.7 percent and 14.4 percent respectively, all paint a picture of broad-based selling across project management, CRM, and productivity-related platforms.

Marketing technology names beyond Braze also featured prominently among the decliners. Klaviyo fell approximately 16.7 percent this week and 20.6 percent over the month, Zeta Global declined 17.0 percent weekly but remains up 16.5 percent over the month, and Sprinklr dropped 13.2 percent weekly and 15.8 percent monthly. LiveRamp declined 10.1 percent on the week and 15.8 percent over the month. This collective underperformance indicates that investors are re-evaluating the entire digital marketing and customer data platform stack, particularly where growth is moderating and competition is intensifying. The market appears to be consolidating exposure toward more scaled, diversified players while de-risking smaller, more specialized names.

The breadth of the drawdown in software and marketing tech suggests that the moves are less about individual companies and more about the asset class. Across vertical software, Constellation Software declined 14.4 percent weekly and 14.2 percent monthly, while Guidewire Software fell 14.2 percent on the week and 18.0 percent over the month. Even ServiceNow, a long-standing quality compounder, declined 10.2 percent this week and 18.6 percent over the month, and Salesforce fell 12.6 percent weekly and 12.0 percent monthly. These moves reinforce that when the market decides to compress software multiples, even the highest-quality names are not immune.

### Biggest Gainers: Semis, Storage, and Energy Stand Out

On the positive side, semiconductors, storage, and energy accounted for many of the largest weekly gainers. Sable Offshore’s 18.3 percent weekly and 120.1 percent monthly rally stands out as the most extreme move, reflecting strong momentum and possibly speculative interest around offshore and energy infrastructure themes. Onto Innovation’s 16.1 percent weekly and 49.3 percent monthly gains highlight strong investor conviction in semiconductor equipment demand, particularly for process control and advanced nodes tied to AI and high-performance compute. Advanced Micro Devices’ 14.1 percent weekly and 17.0 percent monthly rises further cement its status as a core AI beneficiary in the eyes of the market.

Among smaller but high-beta enablers, POET Technologies gained approximately 12.3 percent this week and 39.0 percent over the month, and Astera Labs rallied 11.9 percent weekly and 29.8 percent monthly, underscoring enthusiasm for optical interconnects and connectivity solutions central to modern data-center architectures. Western Digital’s 10.5 percent weekly and 33.2 percent monthly moves, Seagate’s 7.3 percent and 17.5 percent respective gains, and the 9.6 percent weekly and 100.0 percent monthly performance from SNDK within data storage collectively demonstrate a strong bid for storage and memory exposure. This is consistent with the thesis that AI workloads are as much a storage and bandwidth story as they are a compute story.

Industrial and infrastructure names also delivered notable upside. Comfort Systems USA advanced approximately 10.8 percent this week and 26.7 percent over the month, supported by its positioning in mechanical and HVAC systems that are critical to large building and data-center projects. Corning’s 10.5 percent weekly and 10.3 percent monthly performance, GE Vernova’s 9.5 percent and 11.0 percent respective gains, and BWX Technologies’ 8.2 percent weekly and 29.6 percent monthly rise all reflect a market that is increasingly attentive to infrastructure, power, and specialized industrials leveraged to long-cycle spending. Vertiv’s 8.2 percent weekly and 18.1 percent monthly advance is particularly important as it anchors the thesis that power and thermal management are becoming strategic bottlenecks in AI deployment.

These top gainers underscore an equity market that is still willing to embrace risk, but is doing so selectively in areas where structural demand tailwinds are most visible, such as AI hardware, infrastructure, and energy. The key risk is that after such strong monthly moves—especially the triple-digit monthly gains seen in Sable Offshore and SNDK—valuations and expectations may become stretched, increasing the sensitivity to any slowdown in end-market demand or supply-side surprises. For now, however, price action confirms that capital continues to rotate into the physical enablers of AI and energy systems.

### Earnings Recap: A Quiet Period Ahead

From an earnings perspective, the next two weeks are devoid of watchlist company reports, which is unusual for such a broad universe and accentuates the role of macro and factor narratives in driving stock moves. The lack of near-term earnings catalysts means that much of the volatility we are observing, particularly in software and fintech, is likely driven by top-down concerns about valuation, growth sustainability, and interest-rate sensitivity rather than incremental company-specific data. This environment may persist until the next major earnings window, at which point fundamental results and forward guidance can either validate or undermine the current market pricing.

In the absence of imminent earnings, investors will have to rely more heavily on alternative indicators such as management commentary from conferences, product announcements, and peer results outside the watchlist to infer trends. For many of the hardest-hit names—Braze, Atlassian, HubSpot, Intuit, monday.com, and others—the upcoming earnings cycle will be especially important, as it will determine whether these drawdowns represent attractive entry points or a repricing to a new, lower valuation regime. Until then, we expect narratives around AI adoption, enterprise IT spending, and marketing budgets to remain key drivers of sentiment.

## Macro & Rates Environment

### Framing the Macro without New Data

We do not have authoritative, up-to-date macro or interest-rate data within the last week in this report, which constrains our ability to cite specific index levels, yield moves, or inflation prints. However, we can still outline the macro narratives most likely influencing the observed sector rotations and factor moves across the watchlist. The sharp underperformance of high-duration software and fintech, combined with the relative strength of cyclicals, semiconductors, energy, and industrials, is consistent with a market grappling with the path of interest rates, inflation persistence, and the durability of economic growth.

In such environments, investors typically reduce exposure to long-duration assets whose valuations are most sensitive to discount-rate assumptions, such as high-multiple software and early-stage fintech. This helps explain the broad-based drawdowns in application software and marketing technology observed this week, even in the absence of new company-specific news. Conversely, sectors like semiconductors, industrials, and energy often benefit from ongoing capex, industrial production, and commodity demand, which can be more resilient, or even strengthened, under certain macro regimes. The strength in names like Onto Innovation, Advanced Micro Devices, Micron, Nucor, GE Vernova, and Sable Offshore is consistent with investors positioning for continued demand in AI, infrastructure, and energy, even without precise macro datapoints.

### Implications for Risk Premia and Multiples

The pattern of price action across the watchlist suggests that equity risk premia are rising for certain cohorts, particularly software and fintech, while remaining more stable or even compressing for AI hardware and industrials with tangible earnings leverage. When investors start demanding a higher margin of safety for growth, one of the first manifestations is compression in price-to-earnings or price-to-sales multiples for companies perceived as long-duration or highly sensitive to discount-rate changes. The mid-teens weekly drawdowns in Atlassian, HubSpot, Intuit, and monday.com can be interpreted through this lens: even if long-term growth prospects remain robust, the market is less willing to pay peak multiples for that growth.

At the same time, the continued re-rating of semiconductors, storage, and infrastructure names suggests that investors see their earnings profiles as more levered to near-term demand and capex cycles, particularly those tied to AI and data centers. The 60.9 percent monthly gain in Micron, 49.3 percent in Onto Innovation, and 39.0 percent in POET Technologies are extreme examples of how quickly sentiment and valuation can shift when earnings expectations reset higher for structurally favored themes. The risk is that such re-ratings can overshoot, leaving little room for error if demand moderates or competition intensifies.

For portfolio managers, this translates into a need to revisit valuation frameworks and scenario analyses for both growth and cyclical exposures. Stress-testing positions under different rate and growth environments becomes more important when multiples are moving as quickly as they have in recent weeks. Within software, that means favoring companies with clearer paths to profitability, strong free cash flow, and defensible moats, while being cautious on names that rely heavily on long-dated growth projections. Within semiconductors and industrials, it means scrutinizing whether the embedded growth expectations in current prices are realistic and sustainable.

### Sector Sensitivities and Positioning Narratives

The sector performance patterns also provide clues about positioning ahead of upcoming macro or policy events, even without specific dates or figures. The underperformance of diversified banks like Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and JPMorgan, alongside consumer finance names like Synchrony and Global Payments, suggests lingering concerns about credit quality, net interest margins, and consumer health. Meanwhile, the resilience of defensive consumer staples like Constellation Brands, Mondelez, and Clorox points to a bid for stability amid uncertainty.

The relative strength of aerospace and defense names such as Northrop Grumman, which gained 7.8 percent weekly and 18.2 percent monthly, and BWX Technologies, up 8.2 percent weekly and 29.6 percent monthly, may reflect both geopolitical risk considerations and structural demand for defense and nuclear technologies. Power and utilities-related names like GE Vernova and Generac also outperformed, suggesting that investors are increasingly focused on the energy and power underpinnings of digital and AI expansion. These sector sensitivities can inform top-down portfolio tilts even in the absence of fresh macro datapoints.

## Watchlist Deep Dives

### Atlassian (TEAM)

Atlassian’s approximately 19.0 percent decline this week and 26.8 percent loss over the month highlight the severity of the software multiple compression underway. As a collaboration and developer tooling platform with a long runway for growth, Atlassian has historically commanded a premium multiple relative to software peers. The recent drawdown suggests that investors are pushing back on paying such a premium at a time when overall software sentiment is deteriorating. With no imminent earnings on the horizon, the move appears driven by valuation and factor dynamics rather than company-specific disappointments.

For long-term investors, the key questions now revolve around the durability of Atlassian’s growth in core products like Jira and Confluence, its success in monetizing cloud migrations, and its ability to expand margins as it scales. The recent sell-off, while painful, may create an opportunity to add selectively if one believes that Atlassian’s moat and developer-centric distribution model can sustain above-industry growth. However, near-term, the stock is likely to remain sensitive to broader software sentiment and any macro developments that impact IT budgets.

### Braze (BRZE)

Braze’s roughly 23.4 percent weekly and 33.7 percent monthly declines make it one of the most challenged names on the watchlist, particularly within marketing technology. As a customer engagement and messaging platform, Braze sits at the intersection of marketing budgets, data privacy, and digital transformation. The magnitude of the drawdown, absent new earnings, suggests that investors are rethinking the valuation framework for such companies, especially given competitive pressures from both horizontal platforms and larger cloud providers that are increasingly embedding customer engagement capabilities.

From a fundamental perspective, the path forward hinges on Braze’s ability to sustain high growth while improving operating leverage. Investors will also focus on net retention rates, enterprise adoption trends, and the degree to which Braze can differentiate itself through sophisticated orchestration and AI-driven personalization. The current share price weakness may appeal to high-conviction, long-horizon investors, but near-term volatility is likely to remain elevated as the market continues to recalibrate its risk appetite for marketing tech.

### HubSpot (HUBS)

HubSpot’s approximately 16.1 percent weekly and 19.5 percent monthly declines illustrate that even high-quality, scaled platforms are not immune to the software de-rating. As an integrated CRM, marketing, and sales platform with strong execution history, HubSpot had been a core holding for many growth-oriented portfolios. The recent sell-off likely reflects a combination of valuation concerns and questions about the pace of expansion into the upmarket enterprise segment, where competition intensifies against both legacy CRM players and newer entrants.

Looking forward, the investment case for HubSpot still centers on its ability to capture share from legacy systems, cross-sell additional hubs, and drive higher ARPU through advanced features and AI-driven functionality. The recent price weakness could be an opportunity for investors who believe in HubSpot’s long-term franchise value and unit economics, but the stock’s sensitivity to macro concerns around SME and mid-market spend should not be underestimated. As with other software names, the next earnings print will be critical in determining whether the multiple compression has gone too far.

### Intuit (INTU)

Intuit’s decline of approximately 15.7 percent this week and 17.5 percent over the month reflects investor concerns around both macro-exposed consumer and small-business segments and the broader software multiple compression. As the owner of platforms like TurboTax and QuickBooks, Intuit has exposure to tax, accounting, and SMB financial software, which can be both defensive and cyclical depending on the macro backdrop. The recent drawdown may signal fears about consumer pressure, competitive dynamics in tax prep, and the saturation of certain SMB segments.

However, Intuit’s scale, recurring revenue profile, and data assets provide it with strategic advantages that can support long-term value creation. Its ability to cross-sell between its ecosystem, integrate AI and data-driven insights, and expand internationally will be key drivers of future growth. For investors, the sell-off may offer a more attractive entry point, but near-term performance will likely be tied to evolving macro expectations and the market’s broader appetite for large-cap software exposure.

### Nutanix (NTNX)

Nutanix’s approximately 14.5 percent weekly and 8.9 percent monthly declines underscore the market’s more cautious stance on infrastructure software that sits between on-premises and cloud environments. Nutanix has been a high-beta name, benefiting from narratives around hybrid cloud and HCI (hyper-converged infrastructure), but its business model transition and competitive landscape remain points of debate. The recent drawdown may reflect skepticism about the pace and durability of its subscription transformation and concerns about macro-driven enterprise spending slowdowns.

In the current environment, investors will focus on Nutanix’s ability to drive consistent ARR growth, improve profitability, and deepen partnerships with larger ecosystem players. The stock’s underperformance relative to hardware and infrastructure names like Vertiv and Everpure suggests that the market prefers assets with more direct exposure to AI and data-center capex. Nutanix may need to demonstrate clearer linkages to these themes and stronger financial execution to regain investor confidence.

### UiPath (PATH)

UiPath’s roughly 12.1 percent weekly and 10.2 percent monthly declines highlight continued volatility in automation and RPA-related software names. UiPath is positioned as a leader in robotic process automation, but investors remain concerned about competitive intensity, the commoditization of certain automation workflows, and the timeframe needed to translate strong top-line growth into sustainable profitability. The recent de-rating may also be influenced by broader skepticism around software that is perceived as more discretionary or experimental in IT budgets.

For the stock to re-rate positively, UiPath will need to show evidence of expanding use cases, higher engagement within existing customers, and improved unit economics. Its ability to incorporate AI and machine learning into automation workflows, moving beyond simple rule-based tasks, will be a key differentiator. Until then, the stock is likely to trade as a high-beta proxy for broader enterprise automation sentiment.

### Vertiv (VRT)

Vertiv’s approximately 8.2 percent weekly and 18.1 percent monthly gains cement its status as one of the primary ways to express the power and thermal management side of the AI infrastructure trade. With a portfolio spanning critical power, cooling, and data-center infrastructure solutions, Vertiv stands to benefit directly from the rapid growth in AI data-center capacity. The recent performance underscores investor recognition of power and cooling as potential bottlenecks in AI deployment, elevating the strategic importance of Vertiv’s offerings.

The key questions for investors revolve around execution risk, supply-chain management, and the durability of current demand trends. As AI data-center builds accelerate, Vertiv will need to scale its operations while maintaining margins and navigating any potential input cost volatility. The stock’s strong performance also raises the bar for future results, as investors now expect continued upside surprises. Nevertheless, Vertiv remains a core candidate for AI infrastructure exposure, particularly for portfolios seeking diversification away from pure semiconductor plays.

### Micron (MU)

Micron’s performance, up approximately 5.1 percent this week and an impressive 60.9 percent over the month, underscores the centrality of memory and high-bandwidth memory to the AI narrative. As one of the primary suppliers of DRAM and NAND, Micron is highly leveraged to data-center and AI-related demand. The magnitude of the monthly move suggests a rapid reassessment of Micron’s earnings power in a world where AI workloads significantly increase memory requirements per server.

However, memory remains a cyclical industry, and the current enthusiasm must be balanced against the historical volatility of pricing and supply-demand dynamics. Investors will need to monitor capacity expansions, pricing trends, and potential demand fluctuations closely. Nonetheless, the structural shift toward AI-intensive workloads provides a more supportive long-term backdrop than prior cycles, potentially justifying a higher through-cycle valuation multiple than in the past.

### Advanced Micro Devices (AMD)

Advanced Micro Devices’ roughly 14.1 percent weekly and 17.0 percent monthly gains reaffirm its position as a key challenger in AI accelerators and high-performance computing. Investor enthusiasm is driven by expectations for AMD’s GPU and accelerator roadmap, its ability to capture share from incumbents, and the broader secular demand for compute. The stock’s recent performance reflects rising confidence that AMD can translate its technical progress into meaningful revenue and margin expansion.

Risks remain around execution, competitive responses, and the pace of AI workload adoption, but the market is increasingly willing to underwrite a scenario where AMD secures a durable foothold in data-center AI. For portfolio managers, AMD serves as a high-beta, high-upside expression of the AI compute theme, complementing more diversified hardware and infrastructure holdings. Position sizing and risk management are critical given the stock’s volatility and elevated expectations embedded in the recent price action.

### Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM)

Taiwan Semiconductor’s approximately 5.8 percent weekly and 23.6 percent monthly gains highlight its foundational role in the semiconductor ecosystem. As the leading foundry for advanced nodes, TSMC is a direct beneficiary of growing demand for high-performance compute, AI accelerators, and advanced logic chips. The recent performance suggests that investors are increasingly comfortable underwriting a multi-year capex and earnings upcycle driven by AI, even as geopolitical considerations remain in the background.

For long-term investors, TSMC offers a more diversified and lower-volatility way to gain exposure to the AI semiconductor cycle than individual chip designers. However, the stock is not immune to macro or geopolitical risks, and the recent rally implies that expectations for capacity utilization and pricing are already robust. The balance between structural demand tailwinds and external risk factors will continue to shape its risk-reward profile.

### Western Digital (WDC) and Seagate (STX)

Western Digital’s approximately 10.5 percent weekly and 33.2 percent monthly gains, alongside Seagate’s 7.3 percent weekly and 17.5 percent monthly advances, underscore the resurgence of investor interest in storage and HDD/SSD suppliers as AI and data-intensive workloads proliferate. Both companies stand to benefit from increasing storage requirements in data centers, particularly as high-capacity drives and advanced SSDs become increasingly critical to support AI training and inference.

The key debate for these names revolves around the sustainability of the current upcycle, the competitive landscape, and the pace at which AI-driven storage demand can offset potential softness in legacy markets like PCs. The recent performance suggests that the market is leaning toward a more optimistic view of the storage cycle, potentially driven by early evidence of stronger pricing and volume trends. For investors, the risk lies in the inherent cyclicality of the storage market, but the structural AI tailwinds offer a more favorable long-term narrative than in previous cycles.

### Sable Offshore (SOC)

Sable Offshore’s approximately 18.3 percent weekly and 120.1 percent monthly moves make it one of the most explosive names in the universe, emblematic of the kind of torque that can be found in smaller-cap energy and offshore plays. The stock’s performance likely reflects a combination of company-specific momentum, investor enthusiasm for offshore and deepwater exposure, and a broader rotation into energy as a hedge against macro and geopolitical risks.

Such extreme moves require disciplined risk management. While the fundamental backdrop for offshore energy can be constructive, driven by multi-year project cycles and constrained supply, the volatility in names like Sable Offshore is substantial. For most portfolios, position sizing should be conservative, with a clear understanding of the downside if sentiment reverses or if project timelines and capex plans disappoint.

### Comfort Systems USA (FIX)

Comfort Systems USA’s roughly 10.8 percent weekly and 26.7 percent monthly gains highlight investor recognition of its role in mechanical and HVAC systems, including those tied to large commercial projects and data centers. As demand for data-center capacity and high-specification facilities grows, companies like Comfort Systems that provide critical infrastructure services can see multi-year tailwinds.

The stock’s recent performance suggests growing confidence in its backlog, execution, and exposure to structurally growing end markets. The risk lies in the cyclicality of construction and capex, but the AI and digital infrastructure themes provide additional support beyond traditional construction cycles. For investors, Comfort Systems offers an indirect but tangible way to participate in the buildout of the physical infrastructure underpinning AI and cloud growth.

### GE Vernova (GEV) and Generac (GNRC)

GE Vernova’s approximately 9.5 percent weekly and 11.0 percent monthly gains, coupled with Generac’s 5.3 percent weekly and 11.1 percent monthly performance, underscore the growing market focus on power, grid stability, and backup solutions. As AI data centers and electrification trends place increasing strain on existing power infrastructure, companies that provide generation, grid management, and backup power solutions stand to benefit.

Investors are likely viewing GE Vernova and Generac as strategic plays on the energy transition and the power demands of digital infrastructure. The key questions will center on their ability to capture a disproportionate share of incremental demand, manage input costs, and navigate regulatory and policy environments. Their recent performance suggests that the market sees them as important beneficiaries of secular power and electrification themes.

### LPL Financial (LPLA)

LPL Financial’s approximately 5.2 percent weekly and 6.4 percent monthly gains contrast with the broader weakness in diversified banks and consumer finance, highlighting the relative resilience of fee-based advisory and wealth management models. As an independent broker-dealer and wealth platform, LPL benefits from asset growth, advisor recruitment, and the secular shift toward independent advice.

The stock’s outperformance suggests that investors are distinguishing between balance-sheet-intensive financials exposed to credit and net interest margin risk, and fee-based models that are more levered to asset values and flows. For portfolios, LPL can serve as a more defensive way to maintain financial sector exposure while mitigating direct credit risk.

### Constellation Brands (STZ), Mondelez (MDLZ), and Clorox (CLX)

Constellation Brands’ approximately 6.6 percent weekly and 12.1 percent monthly gains, Mondelez’s 3.9 percent monthly advance, and Clorox’s 3.6 percent monthly performance collectively illustrate the relative bid for defensive consumer staples amid volatility elsewhere. These companies offer stable cash flows, pricing power, and resilient demand profiles, which become more attractive when growth and risk assets are under pressure.

The outperformance of these names suggests that investors are rebalancing toward a more barbelled portfolio, combining high-growth AI and infrastructure exposures with stable, defensive consumer staples. The risk for staples lies in valuation, particularly if investors crowd into the space as a safety trade, but their underlying fundamentals remain robust in most macro environments.

### Novo Nordisk (NVO)

Novo Nordisk’s approximately 6.0 percent weekly and 30.5 percent monthly gains highlight ongoing enthusiasm for its diabetes and obesity franchises. While we do not have new clinical or regulatory data within this report, the stock’s performance suggests that the market remains optimistic about the long-term growth trajectory of GLP-1 therapies and their broader metabolic implications.

For investors, Novo Nordisk serves as a core healthcare growth holding with a differentiated product portfolio and strong pricing power. The main risks revolve around competitive dynamics, pricing and reimbursement pressures, and the evolution of long-term safety and efficacy data. However, the recent price action indicates that, at least for now, the market is comfortable underwriting a robust growth profile.

## Upcoming Catalysts

With no watchlist earnings scheduled over the next 14 days, the near-term catalyst calendar is relatively thin for this universe, increasing the importance of macro events, policy developments, and sector-specific newsflows. In such an environment, price action is likely to be driven more by changes in risk appetite, factor rotations, and investor positioning than by company-specific fundamentals. This dynamic can amplify volatility, as we have seen in the past week with software and marketing technology.

For software and fintech, incremental data points may come from industry conferences, management commentary, product launches, and peer results outside the watchlist. Any indications of slowing enterprise IT spending, tightening marketing budgets, or rising churn could further pressure valuations. Conversely, positive signals around AI adoption, platform consolidation, and improved sales efficiency could help stabilize sentiment. In semiconductors and AI infrastructure, news around capex plans from major cloud providers, data-center build-out announcements, and visibility into AI hardware pipelines will be key.

Regulatory and policy developments in areas such as AI governance, data privacy, fintech regulation, and energy policy may also serve as catalysts for specific names or sectors. For example, tighter regulation of digital advertising and data usage could impact marketing technology and AdTech names like Braze, Klaviyo, Zeta, Sprinklr, and The Trade Desk, while favorable energy policies and infrastructure spending could support names like Sable Offshore, Comfort Systems, GE Vernova, Generac, and Nucor. In financials, any shifts in regulatory capital requirements or consumer credit standards could influence sentiment toward banks and consumer finance companies.

Across the board, investor days, strategy updates, and M&A activity could provide idiosyncratic catalysts. In a period with limited scheduled earnings, these unscheduled events take on outsized importance as potential drivers of relative performance. Investors should maintain flexibility and readiness to respond to such developments, particularly in high-beta segments where news can trigger sharp moves.

## What To Watch Next Week

Looking ahead to next week, the key focus areas for the watchlist will revolve around the durability of the recent factor rotation, the behavior of software and fintech after a sharp drawdown, and the sustainability of gains in semiconductors, storage, and energy. In software, we will be closely monitoring whether names like Atlassian, HubSpot, Intuit, monday.com, and Braze find technical support and evidence of stabilization, or whether selling pressure persists. Any signs of bottoming—such as reduced intraday volatility, higher-quality buying on dips, or positive management commentary—could signal that the worst of the multiple compression is behind us, at least in the near term.

In semiconductors and AI infrastructure, the question is whether stocks like Advanced Micro Devices, Micron, Taiwan Semiconductor, Onto Innovation, Astera Labs, and Vertiv can consolidate their recent gains without giving back too much ground. Given the magnitude of the monthly moves, some profit-taking would be entirely rational, but sustained strength would reinforce the view that the AI hardware cycle remains in its early innings. Similarly, in energy and industrials, we will watch whether Sable Offshore, Comfort Systems, GE Vernova, Generac, Nucor, and CNH can extend their momentum, which would further validate the thesis that investors are re-rating hard assets and infrastructure.

In financials and fintech, next week’s price action in Wells Fargo, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Synchrony, Global Payments, BILL, Affirm, Block, and LPL will provide additional insight into how concerned the market is about credit and macro risks. Continued weakness in diversified banks and consumer finance, alongside resilience in wealth platforms like LPL, would reinforce the narrative of a cautious but selective approach to financials. For consumer names, we will track whether e-commerce and digital commerce names like Wix, Global-E, Sea, GoDaddy, and Shopify can find a footing after recent declines, and whether defensive staples like Constellation Brands, Mondelez, and Clorox maintain their relative bid.

Finally, at the portfolio level, we recommend monitoring overall factor exposures—particularly to high-duration growth, AI hardware, cyclicals, and defensives—to ensure alignment with clients’ risk tolerances and investment horizons. The recent week has demonstrated how quickly factor rotations can impact performance, especially in concentrated or factor-tilted portfolios. While the AI and infrastructure themes remain intact, the path forward is unlikely to be linear, and maintaining diversification across growth, cyclicals, and defensives will be essential to navigating the next leg of the market.

In sum, the past week on the watchlist has been a clear reminder that narratives can shift rapidly, even in the absence of new earnings data, and that valuation and positioning always matter. Software and marketing technology have moved from darlings to sources of funding, semiconductors and infrastructure remain in favor as the core expression of the AI boom, and energy and industrials provide cyclical ballast. The coming week will test whether this regime persists, reverses, or evolves into a more nuanced equilibrium as investors digest recent moves and look ahead to the next catalyst window.

Outperformance in defense names like NOC and BWXT, alongside energy names such as SOC and CRC, highlights persistent geopolitical and energy security concerns. Any escalation in regional conflicts or new trade restrictions could disrupt supply chains for semiconductors, industrial components, or energy commodities, amplifying volatility in leaders like TSM, AMD, ONTO, and CIEN. Such shocks could also revive inflation pressures, complicating the macro-policy backdrop for risk assets.

Investors should monitor headlines around strategic chokepoints, sanctions, and export controls, particularly as they relate to advanced chips, critical materials, and shipping routes. While some defense and energy names may benefit fundamentally, the broader equity market would likely face higher volatility and episodic drawdowns. Positioning in supply-chain-resilient companies and diversified sourcing strategies may command a greater premium in this environment.

market_summary:
US equities saw a sharp internal rotation as high-multiple software, ad-tech, and parts of fintech corrected hard while semiconductors, select industrials, and energy/defense outperformed. Macro data and Fed rhetoric kept rates and policy expectations in focus, reinforcing a “higher for longer” bias even as growth remains resilient. Mega-cap tech was mixed, with some AI-levered hardware and data-center names continuing to grind higher while application software and marketing tech sold off.

Factor-wise, profitability and balance-sheet strength outperformed within growth, while long-duration, valuation-stretched names in cloud and vertical software faced multiple compression. Semis, data center infrastructure, and select industrial compounders remain relative leaders, while software indices like IGV traded defensively as investors reassessed AI monetization timelines and IT spending durability. Looking ahead, the tape will key off the next inflation prints, Fed communication, and any signs of moderation in enterprise demand or AI capex, all against a backdrop of thin summer liquidity and elevated single-stock volatility.
